summary: This informational memo suggests ways to measure how quickly a single OSPF router's control plane converges after a change. It focuses on that one router and does not address forwarding plane performance.

eli5.summary: When a road closes, a map app must find a new route. This document describes how to time how fast one router updates its map.

questions: ospf single router control plane convergence
how to measure spf computation time
subtitle: Methods for measuring how fast a single OSPF router adapts to network changes.

tldr.problem: Network operators need consistent ways to measure how quickly OSPF routers react to topology changes, but without standardized tests, different vendors' measurements are not comparable.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4061 defines reference topologies and test methods to measure three core performance areas: LSA processing time, flooding time, and SPF computation time, as well as intra-area convergence behaviors.
tldr.outcome: These benchmarks let operators compare OSPF implementations fairly and predict how routers will perform in their networks.

today: RFC 4061 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted. It remains the standard reference for OSPF single-router convergence benchmarking.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
OSPF is a widely used routing protocol that converges—updates routes—whenever the network topology changes. Network engineers and vendors want to measure how fast this happens, but without a standard way to test, measurements are not comparable across devices. Different testing methods produce wildly different results because they measure different things or measure at different points in the process.

This RFC provides a framework for testing that produces repeatable, comparable measurements. It focuses on control plane convergence—how fast the router's routing table updates—not on how fast data actually travels, which is the forwarding or data plane.
sections.eli5: Before you can say which router is faster, everyone has to agree on how to measure. This document sets the rules for a fair race.

sections.title: Core Performance Tests
sections.content:
The RFC defines three core tests that measure the basic building blocks of OSPF convergence. LSA Processing Time measures how long it takes a router to handle a new routing update (an LSA, or Link State Advertisement). Flooding Time measures how fast the router passes on updates to its neighbors—critical for loop-free networks. SPF Computation Time measures the time required to run Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm and compute new routes.

All three tests measure different aspects of the routing process, and together they reveal where bottlenecks occur in an OSPF implementation.
sections.eli5: The three tests are like timing three parts of an assembly line: how fast one worker processes an item, how fast it passes it down the line, and how fast the final assembly happens.

sections.title: Test Topologies
sections.content:
The RFC defines four reference topologies to allow fair, repeatable testing. Topology 1 is a simple back-to-back setup with one router (the device under test, or DUT) connected to a generator that emulates a network behind it. Topology 2 adds a collector on the other side to measure flooding between the DUT and generator. Topology 3 connects multiple routers to a shared broadcast network (like a LAN) to test designated router election and broadcast behaviors. Topology 4 uses parallel links to test link failure detection.

Each topology isolates different aspects of OSPF behavior and eliminates the need for synchronized clocks across the test network—measurements are taken at a single point.
sections.eli5: Think of them as four different ways to set up a test track: a simple loop, a three-way station, a bus network, and a route with two roads in parallel.

sections.title: Intra-Area Convergence Tests
sections.content:
Beyond basic performance, the RFC defines tests for higher-level OSPF operations on links within a single area. Adjacency formation tests measure how long it takes two routers to become neighbors and exchange their link-state databases. Tests cover both initialization (from a link-down state) and when one router already knows the network topology via other paths. Designated Router (DR) election tests measure the time for OSPF to choose a DR on a broadcast network, which happens every time an adjacency fails.

Convergence tests measure end-to-end time from a topology change (a new link or a link failure) to the router flooding its updated information on the network. Tests distinguish between layer 2 link failures (immediate) and layer 3 failures (detected via hello timeout), which converge at different speeds.
sections.eli5: These tests time bigger events: how long it takes two routers to shake hands, how long to pick a leader on a shared network, and how long to react when links die in two different ways.

sections.title: Testing Methodology
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that tests must run multiple times to yield statistically valid results. A single test run can be skewed by CPU load, cache effects, or timing artifacts. The document uses RFC 2119 requirement words (MUST, SHOULD) to enforce consistent test execution across vendors, ensuring that results are comparable.

Measurements should capture the precise times of key events—when an LSA arrives, when an acknowledgment is sent, when flooding completes—to isolate the component being measured. The RFC also notes that white-box measurements (reading timers from the router itself) can aid understanding but should not be used for vendor comparisons, since different implementations report times differently.
sections.eli5: Good timing means running the same test many times, recording exact moments, and sticking to the rules so any vendor's results can be fairly compared.
